register.name: Medical emergency
register.frequency_sentence: Nearly every household like yours will have someone need emergency care in the next ten years (about 1.4 times a year).

sub_causes.name: Far from emergency care
sub_causes.note: Ambulances take about twice as long to reach rural homes (a median of about 14 minutes against 7).

sub_causes.name: Falls
sub_causes.note: Falls are a leading reason older adults need emergency care; clear floors and light the way at night.

register.name: Wildfire smoke
register.frequency_sentence: Nearly every household like yours will go through days of unhealthy wildfire smoke in the next ten years (about 1.4 times a year).

register.name: Cold wave
register.frequency_sentence: Nearly every household like yours will go through a spell of dangerous cold in the next ten years (about 1.3 times a year).

sub_causes.name: Rolling blackouts in extreme cold
sub_causes.note: Gas supply and power plants fail in deep cold and the grid cuts power in rotation or for days (Texas, February 2021). Already in the county's outage record.

register.name: Stranded in a vehicle
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (63 to nearly all) will be stranded away from home by a crash, breakdown or shutdown in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Black ice or dense fog
sub_causes.note: Chain-reaction crashes and closed highways. Counted in the stranding rate.

sub_causes.name: Transit shutdown or strike
sub_causes.note: Buses and trains stop and commuters without a car are stuck. Counted for commuters who travel by transit.

register.name: Phone or internet outage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 95 (63 to nearly all) will lose phone and internet service for hours in a network outage in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: GPS or radio disruption
sub_causes.note: Space weather or jamming can degrade navigation and timing. Keep a paper map for the way home.

register.name: Strong wind
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 90 (52 to nearly all) will lose power or have damage in a windstorm in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Derecho
sub_causes.note: A fast line of storms with hurricane-force gusts over hundreds of miles; outages can last days. Counted in the windstorm rate.

register.name: Supply chain disruption
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 86 (63–98) will find store shelves empty of things they need in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Fuel shortage
sub_causes.note: Gas stations run dry for days (the Colonial Pipeline shutdown, May 2021, and before hurricanes). It matters most with a generator or a long drive.

sub_causes.name: Cut off: an island or a single road
sub_causes.note: A bridge, ferry or the only road closes and the community is cut off for days. Plan for longer if that is you.

register.name: Winter storm
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 81 (47–99) will be snowed in or lose power in a winter storm in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Blizzard or lake-effect snow
sub_causes.note: Whiteouts or very deep snow close roads for days. Counted in the winter-storm rate.

sub_causes.name: Roof damage under snow
sub_causes.note: Heavy snow or ice loads a roof until it sags or fails. Counted in the winter-storm rate; clear flat roofs early.

register.name: Local water or gas outage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 78 (50–95) will have a water main break or boil-water notice in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Toxic algae in the water supply
sub_causes.note: Algae toxins reach the treatment plant and a do-not-drink order follows (Toledo, 2014). Counted in the water-notice rate.

sub_causes.name: Gas main over-pressure or leak
sub_causes.note: Gas mains over-pressure or leak and homes must be evacuated (Merrimack Valley, 2018). If you smell gas, leave first, then call.

sub_causes.name: Water system failure for weeks
sub_causes.note: A treatment plant or system fails for weeks (Jackson, Mississippi, 2022; Asheville, 2024). The water targets use the county's drinking-water violations to size it.

sub_causes.name: Sewer failure
sub_causes.note: Pumps stop or mains break and toilets cannot be flushed. The sanitation supplies follow the water target.

register.name: Government pay or benefits stop
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 59 will have federal pay stop for two weeks or more in a government shutdown in the next ten years.

register.name: Job loss
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 56 (36–78) will have someone lose a job in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Livestock or poultry disease
sub_causes.note: An animal-disease outbreak (bird flu in dairy or poultry) can hit a farm's income.

sub_causes.name: Recession layoffs
sub_causes.note: Layoffs cluster in downturns; the high end of the job-loss range is a recession year.

register.name: Medicine shortage
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 39 (18–78) will have a daily medicine they cannot fill for days or weeks because of a shortage in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Hospital supply shock
sub_causes.note: A key hospital supply runs short (IV fluids in 2024, after Hurricane Helene closed a plant that makes a large share of the country's supply) and planned care is delayed.

register.name: Heat wave
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 28 will go through a heat wave in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A blackout during a heat wave
sub_causes.note: When the power fails in extreme heat, air conditioning fails for everyone at once. It is the most dangerous combination; where it matters most it is a named scenario.

register.name: A household member is arrested or detained
register.frequency_sentence: For households with people the ages of yours, about 3 in 100 have someone arrested in a year, going by what people tell a national survey (2022–2024); police records suggest up to about 7 in 100. People arrested once are often arrested again, so over ten years fewer households are affected than a year-by-year count suggests. This counts arrests, not guilt or convictions.

register.name: Long illness in the household
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 26 (14–59) will have someone sick at home for weeks in the next ten years.

register.name: Burst pipe or water leak
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 21 (14–30) will have a burst pipe or leak flood part of the home in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Sewer backup
sub_causes.note: Sewage backs up through basement drains; standard home policies leave it out unless you add sewer-backup cover.

register.name: Cyberattack on services
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 18 (7–39) will lose pharmacy, payment or other services to a computer outage or cyberattack in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Critical software failure
sub_causes.note: A faulty update or cloud outage takes down hospital, airline, bank or 911 systems for a day or more (July 2024). Counted in this rate.

sub_causes.name: Card or bank payment outage
sub_causes.note: Cards, bank apps or cash machines stop for hours to days. Keep some cash in small bills.

register.name: Death or disability of an earner
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 16 (10–26) will lose an earner's income to death or disability in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Death in the family
sub_causes.note: A family member who does not earn dies: funeral costs and time off work.

register.name: Chemical spill or release
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 15 (5–34) will be told not to drink the tap water, or to stay inside, after a chemical spill in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Release from a chemical plant
sub_causes.note: A plant that uses large amounts of toxic or flammable chemicals has a release or explosion (West, Texas, 2013). Counted in the chemical-release rate.

sub_causes.name: Train derailment with chemicals
sub_causes.note: A train carrying chemicals derails and burns or leaks; homes within a mile or two are evacuated (East Palestine, 2023).

sub_causes.name: Tanker truck spill
sub_causes.note: A tanker crash closes roads and may bring an order to stay inside nearby.

sub_causes.name: Pipeline rupture
sub_causes.note: A gas or oil transmission pipeline ruptures and burns or spills; nearby homes are evacuated.

sub_causes.name: Refinery, tank farm or port fire
sub_causes.note: A large industrial fire brings orders to stay inside and smoke for days.

sub_causes.name: Chemical spill into the water supply
sub_causes.note: A spill upstream of a water intake brings a do-not-use order for days (Elk River, West Virginia, 2014). Counted in the chemical-release rate.

register.name: Civil unrest
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 14 (4–29) will live under a curfew because of unrest in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Unrest around elections
sub_causes.note: Protests, clashes or curfews around elections or political events.

register.name: Pandemic
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 11 (3–23) will live through a pandemic that changes daily life in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Mosquito- or tick-borne outbreak
sub_causes.note: Local dengue or West Nile spread brings spraying and advisories.

sub_causes.name: Local disease outbreak
sub_causes.note: Measles, hepatitis A or Legionnaires' in the community keeps people out of school or work. Check your vaccinations.

sub_causes.name: Bird flu (H5N1)
sub_causes.note: A candidate pandemic strain that so far passes from animals to people, not between people.

register.name: Break-in
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 10 (5–18) will have a break-in in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Identity theft and disaster scams
sub_causes.note: Accounts opened in your name, or fake contractors and FEMA impostors after a disaster. A credit freeze is free.

register.name: Regional blackout
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 5 (1–14) will lose power in a regional blackout that is not caused by weather in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Attack on power substations
sub_causes.note: Gunfire or sabotage at substations can cut power to a county for days (Moore County, North Carolina, 2022). Utilities report about 78 cases of attack, vandalism or theft a year, most with no outage (2019–2023).

sub_causes.name: Cyberattack on the grid
sub_causes.note: Hackers switched off parts of Ukraine's grid in 2015; no US case has cut power. Utilities report about 7 cyber events a year (2019–2023).

register.name: Hail
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 3 (1–7) will have hail damage their home or car in the next ten years.

register.name: Ice storm
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 3 (1–10) will lose power or be stuck at home in an ice storm in the next ten years.

register.name: Drought
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 3 (1–15) will face water limits in a drought in the next ten years.

register.name: Lightning
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 3 (1–8) will have lightning damage their home or cut their power in the next ten years.

register.name: Flooding from rivers or heavy rain
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 3 (1–7) will have flood water reach their home in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Flash flood
sub_causes.note: Water rises in minutes on roads and near creeks; most flood deaths are people driving into it. Counted in the flood rate; turn around, don't drown.

sub_causes.name: Basement or street flooding in heavy rain
sub_causes.note: Drains overflow and water or sewage comes up into basements outside the mapped flood zone. It is the outside-the-zone part of the flood rate, higher with a basement.

sub_causes.name: Levee failure or overtopping
sub_causes.note: Counted on the dam and levee card, not here: leveed land is mapped outside the high-risk flood zone.

sub_causes.name: Ice-jam flood
sub_causes.note: River ice jams in late winter and backs water into riverside homes. Counted in the flood rate.

register.name: House fire
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 3 will have a house fire in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Carbon monoxide poisoning
sub_causes.note: Carbon monoxide from a furnace, generator or car builds up indoors, most often after storms when generators run too close to the house. Shown beside fires, not added to them; a CO alarm is the defence.

sub_causes.name: Lithium battery fire
sub_causes.note: E-bike, scooter and power-bank batteries can catch fire while charging; charge them where you can see them.

register.name: Tornado
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 2 (fewer than 1 to 5) will have a tornado damage or cut off their neighborhood in the next ten years.

register.name: Wildfire
register.frequency_sentence: Of 100 households like yours, about 1 (fewer than 1 to 4) will have to leave home or lose power because of a wildfire in the next ten years.

register.name: Dam or levee failure
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 730 and 1 in 37 households like yours would be told to leave because a dam or levee fails or threatens to in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Levee failure or overtopping
sub_causes.note: Land behind a levee is mapped outside the high-risk flood zone, so the flood card does not count it; a levee that is overtopped or breaks floods it deep and fast. Counted here.

sub_causes.name: Mine tailings or coal slurry dam failure
sub_causes.note: A mining-waste dam fails and sends slurry downstream. Counted with the other dams in the inventory.

location_factor.label: No high-hazard dam within 10 km lists your ZIP code's towns as the place a failure would flood. About 14 in 100 people in Ward County live behind a levee.

register.name: Earthquake
register.frequency_sentence: About 1 in 1,600 households like yours will feel an earthquake strong enough to knock things off shelves in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Liquefaction
sub_causes.note: Wet, sandy ground turns to slurry in strong shaking; pipes and foundations fail. Water outages last longer where it happens.

sub_causes.name: Fire after an earthquake
sub_causes.note: Broken gas lines and low water pressure let fires spread after a big earthquake. Know how to shut off the gas, and leave it to the gas company to turn it back on.

register.name: Landslide
register.frequency_sentence: About 1 in 3,500 (1 in 15,000 to 1 in 700) households like yours will have a landslide cut off their road or damage their home in the next ten years. About 1 in 35,000 (1 in 77,000 to 1 in 11,000) will have one damage their home.

register.name: War with attacks on US infrastructure
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 250 and 1 in 13 households like yours would lose power, water or phone service for days to attacks in a war in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: Your county has military sites, a big city, a port or a refinery nearby: the kinds of places attacks on infrastructure aim at.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a break-in (about 10 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Outages of power, water or phones for days, and shortages across the country.

register.name: Financial crisis with bank closures
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 200 and 1 in 11 households like yours would have banks close for three days or more in a financial crisis in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Your own bank fails
sub_causes.note: Insured deposits (up to $250,000 per person at each bank) move to another bank, usually within days. The FDIC counts about 23 failures a year (2001–2025), most of them small banks.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a pandemic that changes daily life (about 11 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Cards and bank transfers stop for days.
register.what_it_changes: Keep some cash in small bills (already in your plan) and a second account at another bank (free).

register.name: Very large volcanic eruption
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 130 and 1 in 26 households like yours would live through a year or two of higher food prices after a very large eruption somewhere in the world in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A Yellowstone super-eruption
sub_causes.note: Devastation nearby and ash across much of the country. The USGS puts it at about 1 in 730,000 a year.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a regional blackout (about 5 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: A year or two of higher food prices and some shortages.

register.name: Severe pandemic
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 200 and 1 in 21 households like yours would live through a pandemic far deadlier than COVID-19 in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A natural pandemic as deadly as 1918
sub_causes.note: The 1918 flu killed about 675,000 Americans. Records of pandemics over four centuries give the chance.

sub_causes.name: An engineered germ
sub_causes.note: A germ made or changed on purpose. There is no record to count; it is part of the expert range.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a break-in (about 10 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Months of disruption, strained hospitals and lost income.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing new: the pandemic row already sizes your food and medicine.

register.name: Severe solar storm
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 1,200 and 1 in 24 households like yours would lose power for days to a severe solar storm in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: Your county is at a high geomagnetic latitude (about 56°). Solar storms drive the strongest currents into long power lines nearer the magnetic pole, so the chance of a long outage here is about 2.8 times the national average. The ground's conductivity also matters and is not counted.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a regional blackout (about 5 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Power out for days, and longer where large transformers fail.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing beyond your power plan: a solar storm harms long power lines, not phones or radios.

register.name: Nuclear attack or EMP
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 1,700 and 1 in 26 households like yours would be in a blast zone or under dangerous fallout in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: Limited strike on US territory
sub_causes.note: One or a few weapons on US soil, for example a strike on Guam, Hawaii, Alaska or a West Coast base. It adds to your chance only where your county is a plausible target.

sub_causes.name: A crude nuclear device in a city
sub_causes.note: Heavy damage within about a mile, and everyone within 50 miles told to get inside. It adds to your chance by your metro area's share of FEMA's terrorism-preparedness money.

sub_causes.name: Electromagnetic pulse (EMP) from a high-altitude burst
sub_causes.note: Only as part of a nuclear attack: a burst high above the country could damage electronics and black out a region. EPRI's 2019 study found little damage to large transformers and did not support a nationwide blackout lasting months. The claim that most Americans would die rests on testimony that assumed such a blackout for a year, not on a published model.

sub_causes.name: Disruption across the country
sub_causes.note: Shortages, power cuts and lost income even far from any target. Shown for everyone and never added to your local chance.

sub_causes.name: A nuclear weapon used elsewhere in the world
sub_causes.note: At home: market shocks, shortages and worry, with no fallout of concern. Never added to your local chance.

location_factor.label: Your county has, or is close to, Minot Air Force Base: the Air Force base that runs a nuclear missile field. In a large nuclear war, places like this are treated as likely targets. That does not mean an attack is likely. It means that if one happened, this area would face more danger than most.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a regional blackout (about 5 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: Life-threatening: blast or heavy fallout near likely targets.
register.what_it_changes: One free step: pick your shelter spot at home and at work (a basement, or the middle of the building away from windows).

register.name: Power out for months (any cause)
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 18,000 and 1 in 32 households like yours would be without power for two months or more in the next ten years.

sub_causes.name: A severe solar storm
sub_causes.note: Long outages where large transformers fail; most places would be back within days.

sub_causes.name: EMP from a nuclear attack
sub_causes.note: Only as part of a nuclear attack; EPRI's 2019 study did not support a nationwide blackout lasting months.

sub_causes.name: Attacks on the grid in a war
sub_causes.note: Cyberattacks, sabotage or missiles on power plants and lines.

sub_causes.name: Your county's own outage record
sub_causes.note: Storms and failures like the ones in your county's outage records, with the long tail the records cannot show yet.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a drought that limits your water (about 3 in 100 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: No power for months: water, heat, medicine and money all affected. Puerto Rico waited 328 days after Hurricane Maria.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing to stockpile for months. What helps instead: a way to treat water from a nearby source, a way to cook without power, a plan for toilets and waste, and some cash.

register.name: Mass shooting or bombing
register.frequency_sentence: Between 1 in 330,000 and 1 in 33,000 households like yours would have someone hurt in a mass shooting or bombing in the next ten years.

location_factor.label: The data are too sparse to say where this is more likely, so the chance is the same everywhere.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a landslide (about 1 in 3,500 for you in the next ten years).
register.what_it_changes: Nothing to buy. Two free steps: know "run, hide, fight", and learn to stop bleeding.

register.name: Chemical, biological or radiological attack
register.frequency_sentence: At most about 1 in 50,000 households like yours would be told to stay inside, or to collect medicine at a public site, after a chemical, biological or radiological attack in the next ten years, and perhaps fewer than 1 in 1,000,000.

sub_causes.name: Chemical
sub_causes.note: A toxic chemical released on purpose: shelter inside for hours, or leave the immediate area if told to.

sub_causes.name: Biological
sub_causes.note: A germ spread on purpose (the anthrax letters of 2001): stay home, and collect preventive medicine at a public site if told to.

sub_causes.name: Radiological ("dirty bomb")
sub_causes.note: Shelter inside for hours; the area may stay closed for weeks.

location_factor.label: Ward County is outside the 44 urban areas FEMA funds for terrorism preparedness, so an attack that closes your area is much less likely than in the big cities.

register.anchor_sentence: Less likely than a landslide (about 1 in 3,500 for you in the next ten years).
register.if_it_reaches_you: An order to stay inside for hours, closed buildings, or medicine handed out at public sites.
register.what_it_changes: Nothing beyond your basics: your three-day supplies cover sheltering inside.

frequency_sentences: Households like yours average about 1 emergency-room visit a year (national figures).

buckets.name: Home and personal security
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 20 (15–40) will have a break-in or a nearby curfew at least once in the next 10 years.

Aim for about 2.5 months of income in savings over time, a goal separate from the supplies budget.
This number mostly depends on how long income gaps from losing a job last (expert estimate) and how often job losses happen where you live (expert estimate).
The death or long-term disability of an earner is a question for life and disability insurance, not savings.

buckets.name: Home damaged or uninhabitable
frequency_sentences: Of 100 households like yours, about 4 (3–6) will have to leave home for a while because of damage at least once in the next 10 years.
After a disaster, most displaced households are back within a month, but about 1 in 10 homeowners never return, so insurance and copies of documents matter more than supplies here.

If damage forced you out, 9 in 10 households like yours would be home again within about 7 months; living elsewhere that long costs about $10,000 at 30% of your monthly spending, which loss-of-use insurance pays for.

items.why: Adds 3.8 days of food for 3 people, which completes the 14-day goal. About 3 of 100 households like yours can't get to a store for 10 days or more in the next 10 years. Main causes here: pandemic and wildfire smoke. Paid with $80 saved in earlier months.

savings_track.why: Of 100 households like yours, about 8 (3–15) will have an income gap of more than 3 months in the next 10 years. The goal is about 2.5 months of expenses (about $12,000); you have 1.5 months saved. Your supplies plan is done by month 23. After that, your $80 a month for supplies could go here, reaching the goal in about 7 years from now. This is a savings goal, kept separate from the supplies budget.

requirements.plain: 3 battery lights: a headlamp or lantern for each person aged 4 and over. Use lights, not candles. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
1 pack of AA or AAA batteries for the lights and the radio: one pack lasts a household about 7 days. Check which sizes your lights use. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

1 pair of appliance thermometers, one in the fridge and one in the freezer: after a power cut, keep refrigerated food only if it stayed at 40 °F or below, and throw out perishable food that was above 40 °F for 2 hours or more. (Ready.gov)

Optional: keeping a fridge running takes about 995 Wh a day (a chest freezer about 597) × 2 days = 1,990 Wh. A closed fridge keeps food cold about 4 hours and a full freezer about 48; shelf-stable food avoids the need. (ENERGY STAR, Ready.gov)

For a boil-water notice of up to 2 days: make about 2.6 gallons of drinking water safe each day, about 5.1 gallons in all. To make it safe, boil it for 1 minute (3 minutes above 5,000 feet), or add 8 drops of 6 % unscented bleach per gallon (6 drops of 8.25 %) and wait 30 minutes; double the bleach for cloudy or very cold water. A gas stove can boil water while the gas flows; never use a camp stove or grill indoors. (Ready.gov, PetMD, CDC, EPA; some amounts are estimates)

1 bottle of plain unscented bleach (5 to 9 % sodium hypochlorite, not the splashless kind), for making water safe and for cleaning, however long your target is. At about 0.5 mL a gallon, each ounce treats about 60 gallons of clear water (30 if it is cloudy or very cold), so one bottle treats thousands of gallons. Bleach weakens in storage: buy a fresh bottle every 6 months, when you replace the water you store yourself. (CDC, EPA; some amounts are estimates)

If you boil on a camp stove outdoors, about 0.7 lb of propane brings 19 L to a boil (about 25 to 30 L a pound). Never use a camp stove indoors, and keep no more than 2 one-pound cylinders inside. (EIA, local fire code, CDC; some amounts are estimates)
3 people × 1 gallon a day × 3 days = 9 gallons, plus 0.9 gallons for the dog: about 9.9 gallons. Replace water you store yourself every 6 months. (Ready.gov, CDC, PetMD; some amounts are estimates)

Free first step: fill clean drink bottles you already have with tap water, about 6 gallons, the most a household can usually gather this way. Not milk jugs: they leak. Label them and replace the water every 6 months. (Ready Reckoner research, CDC, Ready.gov, Church of Jesus Christ; some amounts are estimates)
A two-bucket toilet for when toilets can't flush: 2 sturdy buckets with a seat, one for pee and one for poo. (RDPO, Oregon OEM)

Toilet bags: about 0.45 heavy garbage bags a person a day (0.3 to 0.6), counting both bags of a double-bagged load: 3 people × 3 days = 5 bags. Fill halfway, tie, double-bag, and store away from food, water, children and pets. Don't put them in curbside trash or bury them unless officials say so. (RDPO, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)

Cover material for the poo bucket (sawdust, shredded paper, dry leaves or pet bedding): about 1 cup a person a day (0.5 to 1.5) × 3 people × 3 days = 9 cups, about 0.6 gallons. (RDPO; some amounts are estimates)

2 adults at about 2,262 kcal a day each and 1 child aged 4 to 12 at about 1,667 kcal a day: about 6,190 kcal a day × 14 days = 86,700 kcal. These are moderately active needs; the form does not ask sex, so men's and women's needs are averaged. Count calories, not servings. (Dietary Guidelines)

As everyday groceries: about $372 for 42 person-days (USDA Thrifty Food Plan, $8.44 a person a day, plus 5 % for a household of 3). Buy what you already eat, keep it in the pantry and use the oldest first. (USDA)

As bulk staples such as wheat, rice and beans: about $105 ($2.15 to $2.85 a person a day). Cheapest, but it needs cooking and is short on some vitamins, so it suits months rather than days. (Church of Jesus Christ, BYU)

As freeze-dried or dehydrated meals: about $1,040 ($9 to $39 per 2,000 kcal, so $390 to $1,690). They need about 0.6 gallons of extra water a person a day to prepare. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)

A retail "30-day" food kit supplies about 1,290 to 1,730 kcal a day. For the average person here (about 2,063 kcal a day) one lasts about 19 to 25 days, not 30. Compare kits by total kcal. (Dietary Guidelines, retail prices)

Dry food for the dog for 14 days (at least a week): about 0.7 lb a day for each dog = 9.8 lb. Feed what the label says for yours, and keep it in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Food for the dog for 14 days (14 pet-days, at least a week): what it eats now, in an airtight, waterproof container. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)

A way to cook without power, because your plan runs 14 days without a store, longer than food that needs no cooking comfortably covers: your gas range can boil water and cook while the gas still flows. If its igniter needs power, light a burner with a long match (check the manual first). Never use the oven or burners to heat the home. (Oregon OEM, CDC, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

Fuel for a propane camp stove: about 0.2 lb of fuel a person a day × 3 people × 14 days = 8.4 lb, or 9 one-pound propane cylinders. Use the stove outdoors only (carbon monoxide), and store the cylinders outside the living space, with no more than 2 inside the home or an attached garage. (CDC, Ready Reckoner research, EIA, retail prices; some amounts are estimates)

Optional, if you have an outdoor gas grill: a spare filled 20-pound cylinder is the cheapest way to boil water and cook in a long outage. Use the grill outdoors only, away from the house, and keep the cylinder outside, never indoors or in the garage. (local fire code, CDC)
Toilet paper: about 1 roll a person every 5 days × 3 people × 14 days = 9 rolls. Better still, measure a week's use and double it for two weeks. (Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)
Soap for 3 person-months: 3 people × 1 month. Each is 250 g of bathing soap and 200 g of laundry soap, about 1,350 g in all. (Sphere)

Period products for 2 cycles each, about 20 products a cycle (15 to 30). The form doesn't ask sex, so the plan counts half of the 2 people aged 13 to 64 who are not pregnant or nursing: 2 cycles' worth, about 40 products. Keep soap, clean underwear and pain relievers with them, and put used products in a separate bag. (CDC, Sphere, Oregon OEM; some amounts are estimates)
3 warm blankets, one for each person: most homes already have them. (Ready.gov, Sphere)
3 sets of warm layers (coat, hat, gloves, dry socks), one for each person. (Ready.gov, CDC)
An upgrade, not a need: 3 sleeping bags or extra heavy blankets, one for each person. Blankets and warm layers cover a cold target of 2 days. (Ready.gov, Sphere; some amounts are estimates)

A cold plan: pick one room to keep warm, close off the others, put towels under doors and cover windows at night, and find your nearest warming centre in case the home gets too cold. Never heat with a gas oven, grill, camp stove or generator indoors (carbon monoxide). Gas, oil and propane furnaces usually need electricity for their fans and controls, so plan for cold without power. A body temperature below 95 °F needs medical help at once. (CDC, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

1 person takes prescription medicine every day: keep 21 days of it on hand. Keep a written list of each medicine, what it is for and the dose. After a disaster declaration some states let pharmacies give an emergency refill of up to 30 days, and many allow only a few days; ask your pharmacist what yours allows. For medicine the plan keeps at most a month on hand: agencies advise 7 days to two weeks (Red Cross, CDC, Florida), and a longer target is kept up with 60- to 90-day fills from your drug plan (Medicare). (Florida DEM, CDC, Red Cross, Healthcare Ready)

No antibiotics are included in this plan. If you have a specific, foreseeable need, such as remote travel, talk to your own clinician about a standby prescription with written instructions. Never use fish or pet antibiotics, never share prescriptions, and don't use expired ones. (CDC, FDA)
1 battery or hand-crank radio that gets NOAA Weather Radio, with a tone alert, for warnings when phones and power are down. (Ready.gov, NOAA)
Power banks: 2 phones × about 15 Wh a day (10 to 20) × 2 days without power = 60 Wh. Text instead of calling to save battery. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)

2 two-way radios for the 2 people aged 13 and over, to reach each other when phones are down. FRS radios need no licence; GMRS radios reach farther but need a $35 FCC licence that covers the family for 10 years. (FCC; some amounts are estimates)
3 written contact cards, one for each person aged 4 and over: an out-of-area contact, meeting places and key numbers. Phones die; paper does not. (Ready.gov)
1 paper map of your area, marked with meeting places and ways out. Save offline maps on your phone too. (Ready.gov)

Cash in small bills, kept with your documents, because ATMs and cards may not work in an outage: about $240: half of 3 days of your usual spending ($4,800 a month), the part that goes on food, fuel and medicine. No agency gives a dollar amount. (Ready.gov, FEMA; some amounts are estimates)

3 go-bags, one for each person: a sturdy bag you already own will do. Pack copies of documents on paper and on a flash drive, a phone charger, cash, a flashlight, a whistle, an old pair of prescription glasses, a change of clothes and sturdy shoes, and add water, food and medicines from your home supplies rather than buying them twice. You may get only minutes of warning (a local tsunami or a fast fire), so keep the bags packed by the door, and one at work if you work in a danger zone. Practise grabbing them and leaving. Plan where you would stay for about 2 days. (Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Water for the go-bags comes out of the water you store at home, not on top of it: the Red Cross three-day supply for leaving home, about 3 gallons a day for the 3 people × 2 days = 6 gallons. Keep it with the bags or take it as you leave. If you leave on foot, carry what you can (about 2.5 L each) and a filter; the rest goes in the car. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Ready.gov, CDC; some amounts are estimates)

Food for the go-bags comes out of your home food supply, not on top of it: about 6,190 kcal a day × 2 days = 12,400 kcal of food that needs no cooking or refrigeration. (Red Cross, Washington EMD, Dietary Guidelines)

1 pet carrier, one for each pet, with a pet go-kit: water and food from your home supplies, any medicine it takes, records and a photo. Public shelters may take only service animals, so find pet-friendly places to stay ahead of time. (ASPCA, Ready.gov)
Water for the pet go-kit, set aside from your stored water rather than bought extra: 7 days for the dog = 2.2 gallons. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA, PetMD; some amounts are estimates)
Food for the pet go-kit, set aside from your pet food rather than bought extra: 10 days (7 to 10 days) for the dog = 10 pet-days. Replace it every 2 months. (ASPCA)
Keep both vehicles at least half full at all times, and fill up when leaving looks likely. (Ready.gov)

Person 1 travels 13.7 miles (22 km) by car to work or school; walking home at about 3 mph takes about 4.6 hours. Keep a get-home bag in the car: comfortable walking shoes, a light, a paper map, cash in small bills, a rain or warm layer, and water and snacks from home. Be ready to stay at work for 24 hours if you can't leave. (FHWA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Water for person 1's walk home: 4.6 hours × about 0.5 L an hour = 2.3 L, in a bottle filled from home rather than bought extra. (FHWA; some amounts are estimates)

Snacks for person 1's walk home: about 500 kcal for 4.6 hours on foot (about 1,250 kcal every 12 hours), from your food at home rather than bought extra. (FHWA, Dietary Guidelines; some amounts are estimates)

Person 2 travels 3.1 miles (5 km) by car to work or school; walking home at about 3 mph takes about 1 hour. Keep a get-home bag in the car: comfortable walking shoes, a light, a paper map, cash in small bills, a rain or warm layer, and water and snacks from home. Be ready to stay at work for 24 hours if you can't leave. (FHWA, Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Water for person 2's walk home: 1 hour × about 0.5 L an hour = 0.5 L, in a bottle filled from home rather than bought extra. (FHWA; some amounts are estimates)

Snacks for person 2's walk home: about 100 kcal for 1 hour on foot (about 1,250 kcal every 12 hours), from your food at home rather than bought extra. (FHWA, Dietary Guidelines; some amounts are estimates)

2 car emergency kits: jumper cables or a charged jump pack you have tried, a flashlight, warm clothes, a blanket, bottled water and snacks, and your roadside-assistance number on paper; sand or cat litter in snow country. (Ready.gov)

1 family first-aid kit for 3 people: the Red Cross list for a family of 4 (bandages, gauze, tape, antiseptic wipes, gloves, a breathing barrier, a cold pack, tweezers, an emergency blanket and a thermometer). Add your own medicines and emergency numbers, and replace what you use. (Red Cross)

1 package of each of 4 kinds of non-prescription medicine (a pain reliever, an anti-diarrhea medicine, an antacid and an allergy medicine): one package of each lasts about 14 days for 4 people. That is 4 packages for 14 days. Follow the label, and ask a pharmacist about children's versions. (Ready.gov, CDC, Red Cross; some amounts are estimates)
1 oral thermometer (non-mercury, non-glass; it is on the Red Cross kit list). (Red Cross)

Oral rehydration salts for vomiting, diarrhea or heat illness: 3 packets a person for every 2 weeks, at least 2 weeks' worth. For 3 people and 14 days that is 9 packets. Mix each packet into 1 litre of safe water. (CDC; some amounts are estimates)
1 bleeding-control kit: a tourniquet and a pressure bandage for serious bleeding, and a Stop the Bleed class so you know how to use them. Serious bleeding can kill before help arrives. (DHS)

A wound-care and splint add-on for the first-aid kit: an irrigation syringe to wash a wound with clean water, wound-closure strips, an elastic wrap, a padded splint, trauma shears, blister dressings and gauze for packing a deep wound. Washing a wound out with plenty of clean water is the key step. Your plan runs past 14 days without a store, when a small wound has to be cared for at home. (Wilderness Medical Society, Red Cross; some amounts are estimates)

A fire escape plan: two ways out of every room, a meeting spot outside, and a practice run with everyone. Upstairs bedrooms need a second way out, such as a window onto a porch roof or an escape ladder (see the ladder line). Test your smoke alarms every month. (Ready.gov)

No fire extinguisher yet: 2 multipurpose (A-B-C) extinguishers, one on each of the 2 floors a home like yours has, the ground-floor one near the kitchen. If your kitchen is on another floor, keep one there too. Learn how to use one before you need it. Small home fires are common: CPSC estimated about 6.6 a year for every 100 households, most of them cooking fires, and fire departments attend only about 3 in 100 of them. (USFA, CPSC; some amounts are estimates)

A house like yours usually has bedrooms upstairs (2 levels): 1 two-storey escape ladder for an upstairs bedroom window, in case fire or smoke blocks the stairs. Skip it if every bedroom is on the ground floor or already has a second way out, such as a porch roof. Keep it by the window and practise with it. (Ready.gov; some amounts are estimates)
Swap phone numbers with 2 neighbours and agree who checks on whom after a storm or an outage, when phones and roads may be down. (an estimate)

N95 respirators, for about 5 days of smoke, dust or ash: 1 a day for each of the 2 people aged 13 and over = 10 respirators. A well-fitting N95 protects far more than a cloth or surgical mask; replace it when breathing through it gets harder. Respirators are not made to fit young children (EPA): for them, the clean room is the protection. (CDC, EPA; some amounts are estimates)

1 portable air cleaner with a HEPA filter for your clean room: for a room of about 200 square feet, a clean air delivery rate (CADR) of at least 130 for smoke (EPA's sizing, more for high ceilings). Keep a spare filter, and avoid air cleaners that make ozone. (EPA; some amounts are estimates)

Cheaper than an air cleaner: a 20-inch box fan with a 20 by 20 inch MERV 13 filter taped to its intake side, which EPA calls a cost-effective way to cut smoke indoors. Use a newer fan with safety features, and do not leave it running while no one is home. (EPA)

A clean-room plan for smoky or dusty days: pick one room with few windows and doors where everyone can sleep, keep it closed, set the heating or cooling to recirculate (or turn off fans that pull in outside air), run the air cleaner there, and do not fry food, burn candles or vacuum on those days. Children stay in the clean room: respirators do not fit them. (EPA, CDC)

Savings goal: about 2.5 months of expenses ($12,000 at $4,800 a month), built up over time and kept apart from the supplies budget. You have about 1.5 months saved now. Planners often suggest 3 to 6 months; the CFPB says it depends on your situation. (FINRA, St. Louis Fed, CFPB)

Copy the 4 parts of FEMA's Emergency Financial First Aid Kit: IDs, financial and legal papers (including insurance), medical information, and household contacts. Keep copies in a waterproof, fire-resistant place or with someone you trust, with photos of your home and belongings, and update them once a year. (FEMA)

Home and renters policies usually don't cover floods. Decide on flood insurance before you need it: Most homes in your county are outside the mapped high-risk flood zone, and that is where many uninsured floods happen: about 3 in 10 flood insurance claims come from outside high-risk flood areas. A quote costs nothing, and a new policy usually starts 30 days after you buy it. It pays up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings. (FEMA, FloodSmart, Ready.gov)

Your home has a basement. Most home policies pay little or nothing for water that backs up through the drains or a sump pump that overflows: ask your insurer what a sewer and drain backup endorsement would cost, and decide. (NAIC)

warnings.message: Not enough food stored by month 3 in case pay or benefits stop.
warnings.why: Government pay and food benefits have stopped before, for days to weeks at a time, during shutdowns and funding lapses. A small store of food built early bridges the gap; a food bank or 211 can help too.

warnings.message: The plan counts everyday basics most homes already have: a charged mobile phone: alerts, calls and a backup light, go-bag for each person: a backpack you pack from your supplies, manual can opener, a cooking pot with a lid, three days of the food you normally eat, a warm blanket for each person and warm layers for each person: a coat, hat and gloves.
warnings.why: Most homes have these, so the plan does not ask you to buy them. If any is missing, untick "Assume everyday basics" on the Have screen, or list the item as not owned, and the plan will add it.

This binder is your household's plan on paper, for when phones, power or the internet are down. Keep it where everyone can find it, and keep the contact page with you too.

para.t: Save 988 in every phone. It offers free, judgment-free support 24/7 for mental health, substance use and more, by call, text or chat.

para.t: Pick a spot for each danger below, at home and at work, and practice going there.
In a high wind or severe thunderstorm warning, go inside a sturdy building, to an inside room or basement.
Stay away from windows while damaging wind is near.
A safe room or storm shelter is best; next is a small inside room with no windows on the lowest floor.

para.t: Of 100 households like yours, about 10 (8–15) will have to leave home quickly at least once in the next 10 years. Warning can be as short as a few minutes (a home fire) or as long as 12 hours. For chemical spills and releases, plan for as little as a few minutes of warning; for wildfires, 15 minutes. Plan to be away for about 2 days. Most evacuations last a few days, but after a home fire you could be away for 2 months or more.

# Prepare: what to do before

**For:** 2 adults and 1 child, with 1 dog  
**Where:** Ward County, North Dakota (ZIP code 58701)  
**Home:** an owned house, with a basement, city water, gas heat and central air conditioning  
**Plan date:** October 1, 2026  
**Ready for:** very serious disruptions (the 1-in-100 setting), in today's climate. Water is planned at the basic level, about 1 gallon a person a day.[1]

> Ready Reckoner is an independent, open-source planning aid. It is not official emergency guidance, and not medical, legal or financial advice. Follow instructions from your local officials first.

## Summary

**Where you are now:** getting started. **What is enough for your risks:** one month of supplies. At your budget, the bare minimum (three days of water, light, warmth and medicine) is in place by month 2 (December 2026), and everything by month 23 (September 2028). Start with the free steps under Your plan.

**What the plan assumes you already have:** a charged mobile phone, go-bag for each person, manual can opener, a cooking pot with a lid, three days of the food you normally eat, a warm blanket for each person and warm layers for each person. If any is missing, untick "Assume everyday basics" on the Have screen and the plan will add it.

## Your plan

Your budget is $80 a month, plus $300 once at the start. Free steps come first, then what protects you most for each dollar (water, medicine and safety first), until every need has enough.[2]

### Start now: free steps (from October 1, 2026)

- [ ] Set up emergency alerts and know how to reach 911
- [ ] Make a household plan and a contact card for each person
- [ ] Fire safety at home
- [ ] Tap water in clean reused bottles
- [ ] Keep medicines going
- [ ] Water and food know-how
- [ ] Plan how you would leave
- [ ] Neighbours and skills

### Safety rules to learn now

- **Fire:** Know two ways out of every room. Once you are out, stay out, and call 911.[3, 4]
- **Gas:** If your gas was shut off, only the gas company or a professional should turn it back on.[5]
- **Water heater:** Turn off its power or gas before you drain it for water.[5]
- **Food:** In a power cut, throw out food that has been at 40°F or warmer for 2 hours.[6]
- **Generator:** Run it outside, 20 feet from windows and doors. Never plug it into a wall outlet or the house wiring: that can electrocute utility workers and neighbors.[6, 7]
- **CPR:** Take a first-aid and CPR class.[8]

### This month

- [ ] **Extra supply of daily prescription medicine**: 10 days of one person's medicine, about $9 (usually $4–13)
- [ ] **Store-bought bottled water**: 4 gallons, about $4
- [ ] **Unscented household bleach (for treating water)**: 1 bottle, about $8
- [ ] **Multipurpose fire extinguisher**: 2 extinguishers, about $67 (usually $45–89)
- [ ] **Bleeding-control kit (tourniquet and pressure bandage)**: 1 kit, about $71 (usually $48–95)
- [ ] **Family first-aid kit**: 1 kit, about $36
- [ ] **Get-home bag for each commuter: a small bag you stock from home**: 2 bags, about $69
- [ ] **Extra pet food in an airtight container**: 5 pounds of dry food, about $6 (usually $4–9)
- [ ] **N95 respirators for teens and adults**: 10 respirators, about $10 (usually $7–13)
- [ ] **Extra toilet paper**: 9 rolls, about $7 (usually $4–10)
- [ ] **Period products for two cycles**: 2 cycles' supplies, about $12 (usually $9–15)

### Next month: Month 1 (from November 1, 2026), $80 to spend

- [ ] Clean-room plan for smoky, dusty or chemical air
- [ ] Get the toilet and hand washing ready
- [ ] Practice: ten-minute drills and the first things to do
- [ ] When a storm, freeze or heat wave is forecast: the 48-hour list
- [ ] Pet plan
- [ ] Legal readiness
- [ ] Mental health
- [ ] Documents and insurance
- [ ] Keep your vehicle ready
- [ ] **Extra supply of daily prescription medicine**: 11 days of one person's medicine, about $10 (usually $4–15)
- [ ] **Plastic sheeting and duct tape to shelter in place**: 1 kit, about $32
- [ ] **Refrigerator and freezer thermometers**: 1 pair, about $8 (usually $5–11)
- [ ] **Bar soap and laundry soap**: 3 person-months, about $18 (usually $6–30)
- Set aside $8 toward **personal radiation dosimeter card**.
- [ ] **Decide this month** (see Documents and money): ID for every person (passport book or card, or a state ID); flood insurance, even outside a flood zone; sewer and drain backup cover for a basement; a stronger roof when you re-roof (FORTIFIED); a backflow valve and a battery-backup sump pump.

### After that

From month 2 the plan follows Checklists, free steps first; each line gives its month.

### The rare-event allowance

- **Personal radiation dosimeter card** (month 4, about $25): Paid from your rare-event allowance ($8 a month, a tenth of your monthly money), after your three-day basics. It is for the nuclear attack or EMP row you ticked: where you live, more than 1 in 1,000 households like yours face it in 10 years, the least the allowance needs. Your basics cover the rare rows it does not buy for. Paid with $24 saved in earlier months.
- **Shielded (Faraday) bag for spare electronics** (month 12, about $68): Paid from your rare-event allowance ($8 a month, a tenth of your monthly money), after your three-day basics. It is for the pulse from a nuclear attack, part of the nuclear attack or EMP row you ticked: where you live, more than 1 in 1,000 households like yours face it in 10 years, the least the allowance needs. Your basics cover the rare rows it does not buy for. Paid with $63 saved in earlier months.

### When you are done

Every need is covered by month 23 (September 2028). After that, keep up the maintenance calendar and put the same money toward savings.

### Things to watch

- **Worth acting on: Not enough food stored by month 3 in case pay or benefits stop.** Government pay and food benefits have stopped before, for days to weeks at a time, during shutdowns and funding lapses. A small store of food built early bridges the gap; a food bank or 211 can help too.

## Documents and money: decisions and savings

### Decisions

- [ ] **Decide: ID for every person (passport book or card, or a state ID).** A passport book or card for each person, children included, proves who you are and your citizenship if other papers are lost, and the card shows no home address; get them before you need them. The federal fee schedule: a first adult book $165 and card $65 ($130 and $30 plus a $35 acceptance fee), for children under 16 a book $135 and card $50 (22 CFR 22.1).[20, 21, 22]
- [ ] **Decide: flood insurance, even outside a flood zone.** Home and renters policies usually don't cover floods. Decide on flood insurance before you need it: Most homes in your county are outside the mapped high-risk flood zone, and that is where many uninsured floods happen: about 3 in 10 flood insurance claims come from outside high-risk flood areas. A quote costs nothing, and a new policy usually starts 30 days after you buy it. It pays up to $250,000 for the building and $100,000 for belongings.[23, 24, 25, 26, 27]
- [ ] **Decide: sewer and drain backup cover for a basement.** Your home has a basement. Most home policies pay little or nothing for water that backs up through the drains or a sump pump that overflows: ask your insurer what a sewer and drain backup endorsement would cost, and decide.[28]
- [ ] **Home repairs to weigh when the time comes:** a stronger roof when you re-roof (FORTIFIED); a backflow valve and a battery-backup sump pump. Some come with grants or insurance discounts: ask your state emergency management office and your insurer.[28, 29, 30, 31]

### Savings

Of 100 households like yours, about 8 (3–15) will have an income gap of more than 3 months in the next 10 years. The goal is about 2.5 months of expenses (about $12,000); you have 1.5 months saved. Your supplies plan is done by month 23. After that, your $80 a month for supplies could go here, reaching the goal in about 7 years from now. This is a savings goal, kept separate from the supplies budget.
